lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s 101 on trade and tariffs
lead.head: Trade 101, for a world on the boil
body: For weeks, listeners had asked Amit Varma and Ajay Shah for an episode on Donald Trump’s tariffs and the trade wars. Varma’s first instinct was that the two had already said it all, over decades of writing and thinking.

But people consume their work piecemeal, he said. So the hosts set out to build a 101: why globalisation is good and tariffs are bad, from first principles, and how trade, and thinking about it, evolved through history.
The chaos of the present was left for the next episode.
Shah framed the stakes. Economics, populism, trade and international relations were “coming together into a boil”, he said. “What happens here will matter for many many years to come.”
## Seven reasons

Varma brought seven reasons why globalisation is great, reasons both hosts hold. The first was moral, and he expected many to reject it: “If you and I want to associate with each other in any way that is voluntary, who is anybody else to stop us?” {095-C01}

The next four were economic. Voluntary trade is positive-sum, so buyer and seller both say thank you. Comparative advantage means a country need not be the best at anything to gain, Shah said, because what counts is the ratio of superiority.
A bigger market brings scale and specialisation. And growth spreads across borders, as one country’s rising middle class becomes another’s market.

The last two were cultural. Everything Indians consider their own, Varma argued, from food and clothes to languages, came from somewhere else. {095-C08} The potato, the chilli and the guava arrived through the Columbian Exchange.
The seventh, Shah’s, built on Jagdish Bhagwati: a closed economy sets its elites fighting over a fixed pie, while an open one points them at the world.
## A history with a warning
The history ran from the Silk Road, through colonial trade that was not really free, to the mercantilists, who hoarded gold and saw imports as gold sent away.
Adam Smith and David Ricardo flipped the frame. A country exports, Shah said, only so that it can import the wonders of the world. {095-C11}

By 1909 the first wave of globalisation seemed so settled that Norman Angell declared war impossible. The First World War followed. After the Smoot-Hawley tariffs of 1930, Shah traced lines all the way to the second.
India’s own story ran from decades of import substitution to the opening of 1991. Shah called the fourfold rise in GDP from 1991 to 2011 India’s greatest economic achievement in 10,000 years.
## Four myths, busted

The hosts then took apart four myths. Exporters do not pay tariffs; a country’s own consumers do. A trade deficit is accounting, not a loss. Tariffs hurt the very industries they claim to protect. And goods are no more special than services.

On most of what the Trump administration does, Varma said, there are reasonable arguments on both sides. Not here. “On tariffs on this stuff, there is absolutely no argument on the other side.” {#noargument}
His own policy would be simple: India should take its tariffs to zero on everything, whatever other countries do, because a tariff hurts a country’s own people. {095-C15}
For homework, Varma prescribed Thomas Sowell’s *Basic Economics* and Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson*. Shah named a single book: Jagdish Bhagwati’s *In Defense of Globalization*.

second.label: The first globalisation
second.head: The war that couldn’t be
second.deck: Norman Angell said trade had made war impossible. The next decade disagreed
body: The first wave of globalisation, built on the ideas of Adam Smith and David Ricardo, seemed settled. In 1909 Norman Angell argued in *The Great Illusion* that war was now impossible, because nations were too intertwined by trade. {095-R10}

Amit Varma asked listeners to mark the date. The First World War followed. John Maynard Keynes recalled the lost world in *The Economic Consequences of the Peace*: in 1914 a Londoner could order the products of the whole earth by telephone, sipping his morning tea. {095-R09}

The war made people cynical and led to disastrous decades, Varma said. The mistake was believing that free trade was now a done deal, and he admitted that he and Ajay Shah had believed it too. {095-S07}

quote.text: You thought the game was over, this is settled, this is good for humanity, didn’t work out that way.

second.caption: the book that ruled out war

third.head: The bus the tigers caught
body: Around 1950, Amit Varma said, India was doing really well compared with South Korea and Taiwan. “We should have been the ones who succeeded, who had embraced democracy, who had so many good things going for them.” {095-S03}
But India kept its markets closed. The East Asian Tigers opened theirs, achieved economies of scale and, competing with the rest of the world, lifted their standards. They took off.

Through the 1960s and 1970s, Varma said, India could have used its cheap labour for manufacturing at scale. It missed the bus because of terrible labour laws and terrible industrial laws. {#missedbus} Bangladesh, he said, is winning today because it embraced that path.
India later found a niche in services, partly because it had many English-educated people for outsourcing jobs.

p2.title: The case for trade
p2.deck: Seven reasons, a short history and four myths, in Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s 101

sections.label: The first reasons
sections.head: Who is the state to stop us?
sections.caption: the freedom to trade
body: Amit Varma offered seven reasons why globalisation is great. The first, he said, is moral: if two people trade voluntarily and nobody else’s rights are infringed, nobody has any business getting in the way, whether one is in India and the other in Washington, DC. {095-C01}

Ideologies are incoherent here, he said, defending freedom in the bedroom but not the marketplace, or the reverse. Ajay Shah wanted the point up front: calling Pune or Mozambique to strike a deal is the same act.
## Better at nothing, still better off
Every voluntary trade is positive-sum, Varma said, unlike tennis, where one player wins only if the other loses. The key word is voluntary: colonial extraction was not free trade. {095-C02}

To explain comparative advantage, Varma asked listeners to assume Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma were the best drivers in Bombay. “Actually they’re not. I am,” he said. They should still hire a chauffeur and keep their minds on cricket and acting. {095-J01}

Shah gave David Ricardo’s version: even if Portugal is better than England at both cloth and wine, both end up with more of each by specialising and trading. A poor country, he said, need not be the world’s best at anything. {095-C03}

~ Scale was the fourth reason. With ten customers for shirts, Varma said, you get them made by hand; with the whole world, you can invest on a completely different scale, raise quality and bring costs down. {#tenshirts}

quote.text: Every voluntary action between two consenting adults is always a positive sum game.

sections.label: The cultural case
sections.head: Imported, and all ours
sections.caption: why every culture is borrowed
body: Two of the seven reasons were cultural. Everything Indians consider quintessentially their own, Amit Varma said, from clothes to food to languages, came from somewhere else and melded together. {095-C08}

The Silk Road carried religions along with goods. Islam, Varma said, did not first reach India with invaders: during the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad himself, Muslims came to the south as traders. {095-S02}

The Columbian Exchange brought the potato, the chilli and the guava. Varma read from a World Economic Forum piece: “Imagine Italian cuisine without tomatoes, which came from the new world, or Irish history without the potato.” {095-J18}
## Fewer knives drawn

The second, Ajay Shah’s, was about political economy, building on Jagdish Bhagwati, Srinivasan and Krueger. In a closed economy, he said, elites see a finite landscape and fight to grab a slice of the pie. {095-C09}
Open it up, and the game becomes the world. Elites see eye to eye on policies that make the country strong, and the levels of conflict go down.
~ Better things get done, Shah said, because elites compete in a positive way “rather than in a negative way of trying to put the knife into each other”.

quote.text: It would be such a shallow world if we become like North Korea, put up a high wall, and get stuck in one culture.

sections.label: The history of ideas
sections.head: Kings who hoarded gold
sections.caption: mercantilism and Adam Smith
body: From the 16th to the 18th century, Amit Varma said, trade was seen through mercantilist eyes. A king wanted gold and silver in his treasury, so exports were good, imports bad, and the aim was always a surplus. Donald Trump, he said, holds that view today.
Even the age of exploration did not bring free trade. Colonialism made it extractive: for a long, long time, Spanish America could trade freely only with Spain. {#spanish}
In America, Alexander Hamilton, “a bit of a mercantilist”, popularised the case for protecting infant industries; Jefferson, Varma said, was “more of a freedom guy”. {095-J15}
## Wonders from overseas

Ajay Shah explained the turn. England grasped that the privilege of trade lies in buying from others, and that a country exports to earn the means to import. His Casio wristwatch, bought for all of 1,100 rupees, would not have been possible without the ability to buy from overseas. {#casio}
Varma, who distrusts the great-man theory of history, made an exception for Adam Smith. “Adam Smith is to economics, what Charles Darwin is to biology,” Shah said. {095-J13}
~ In 1843, Varma added, *The Economist* was founded to defend free trade. It still calls itself a newspaper, he noted, “for some reason”. {095-J10}

quote.text: There’s no fun in exporting. The real fun is in importing.

sections.label: The India story
sections.head: Opened up, grew fourfold
sections.caption: India’s opening up
body: For decades, Amit Varma said, India was completely closed, because its leaders believed it must be self-reliant. The idea, he said, was then called import substitution.
What Nehru did and what Modi is doing are much the same, he said: “one is a successor of the other in terms of bad economic thinking. In other ways they are very, very, very different.” {095-J07}

Then came 1991. From then until 2008, Ajay Shah said, India only reduced its trade barriers and capital controls, and it got the best economic performance in its history. The connection, he argued, is causal, not random. {095-C19}
## A freedom story

Varma stressed that the golden years straddle parties. The Congress kickstarted them under Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh, the Vajpayee government got many things right, and governments after 2008 got many things wrong.
Growth, he argued, is a moral matter. Their friend Nitin Pai reckoned each 1 per cent rise in GDP takes a million people out of poverty, later revising it to two million. {095-C07}
~ “It is okay for elites to sit in their air conditioned rooms sipping their single malt to talk about neoliberal values,” Varma said. Growth, he said, is what puts food on plates. {095-J08}

quote.text: The greatest ever economic achievement of India in the last 10,000 years was the 4x gain of GDP that happened from 1991 to 2011.

sections.label: Busting myths
sections.head: The foreigner doesn’t pay
sections.caption: who really pays a tariff
body: Donald Trump says foreigners pay the tariffs. Ajay Shah had never heard the idea in his life, he said, “until one low IQ American president said it”. {095-J04}
A 100-rupee part comes into India, the government charges a 10 per cent tariff, and it sells for 110 rupees. The Indian consumer pays. {095-C13}
Nor does it stop there. If a 500-rupee foreign shirt becomes 550, Shah said, every Indian maker of the same shirt will charge 550 too.
## A tax on your own poor

For Amit Varma, tariffs are always a tax on a country’s own poor. Every interference in free markets, by what he jokingly calls Varma’s law, moves wealth from the poor to the rich. In his example, a local maker pleads with the government: “See, I’m crying, I’m an infant, protect me.” {095-J05}
So “reciprocal” tariffs make no sense. Varma quoted the economist Joan Robinson: other countries putting rocks in their harbours is no reason to put rocks in ours. {#robinson}
~ He would take India’s tariffs to zero on everything, whatever others do. It is not about the other country, he said, but about its own people. {095-C15}

quote.text: A tariff is an attack on your own people.

sections.label: More myths
sections.head: In the red with the babysitter
sections.caption: trade deficits and services
body: The word deficit sounds like a loss, Ajay Shah said, but in trade it is arithmetic. In the market for tomatoes, the tomatoes bought always equal the tomatoes sold, after the event. So it is in the market for dollars.

A foreigner buys Indian shares, an Indian buys a house in London, Amit Varma imports cans of Diet Coke. Capital flows and trade flows must add up to zero, so an investment boom that brings capital in brings a trade deficit with it. {095-C16}
Varma added that individuals trade, not countries. Tim Harford has a trade deficit with his babysitter: he pays her, she buys nothing from him, and both are better off. {095-R14}
## Bearings and call centres
Shah had never understood the appeal of goods. Some people, he said, have an “almost mystical attachment to goods” because you can touch and feel a car. {#mystical}

Before fibre-optic cables, services could not be traded; now they can, so global law firms should work in India and Indian firms abroad. “There is no reason to think that a ball bearing is somehow better or superior than a call centre call,” he said. {095-C18}
~ Varma agreed, but feared Donald Trump would take the lesson to tariff services too. “And it will be your fault,” he told Shah. {095-J06}

quote.text: It’s an accounting fact that if you have capital coming into a country, you will always have a deficit on the trade account.

side.boxText: Jagdish Bhagwati’s *In Defense of Globalization* is the one book Ajay Shah names on the subject. Bhagwati’s work with Srinivasan and Krueger also lies behind Shah’s argument that openness calms a country’s quarrelling elites. {095-R05}

contQuote.text: It is very important to see trade not just as a lovely way to harness comparative advantage and prosperity, but also to stop the madness of nationalism and war

stories.caption: the tariffs behind the Depression
stories.kicker: Amit Varma, after Thomas Sowell, on the Great Depression
stories.head: Down to 6.3%, then the tariffs
body: In the popular imagination, the Great Depression began with the stock market crash of October 1929. {#crash} Amit Varma, drawing on one of his favourite writers, Thomas Sowell, told it differently.
The crash was an event, Varma said. People lost jobs and companies shut down. But it was not what really brought about the Depression.
A couple of months after the crash, unemployment peaked at 9 per cent. {#unemp} Then it started to decline. By June 1930 it was down to 6.3 per cent.

That was when President Hoover decided to lift employment. His idea, Varma said, was “classical zero sum mercantilist Donald Trumpish thinking”: put tariffs on the outside world, and domestic manufacturers would build more factories and bring the jobs back.
So came the Smoot-Hawley tariffs. The world reacted, as of course it would, with reciprocal tariffs of its own, and a trade war followed in which everybody suffered.
“Within five months, the unemployment shoots back up to over ten percent, and for the rest of the nineteen thirties, it is a double digit figure,” Varma said. {095-S05}
America moved into the Great Depression and did not manage to come out for a long time.

~ Sowell, now 94, had warned about Smoot-Hawley decades ago. Recording on 15 April, Varma reported that Sowell had just given an interview on Donald Trump’s tariffs. {#sowell94} Varma put Sowell’s message this way: “It’s the same damn thing happening again.”
stories.why: In Varma’s telling, the crash did not turn a downturn into a decade of disaster; the policy response did. Shah drew the lesson for trade wars: “An eye for an eye leaves the whole world blind.” {095-J12}

stories.caption: the road from tariffs to war
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a tariff war became a shooting war
stories.head: From tariff wall to world war
body: After Smoot-Hawley, Ajay Shah recalled, global trade fell by about 66 per cent. He drew lines from those tariffs all the way to the Second World War. {095-S06}
The first runs through politics. Economic hardship destroys the centre, he said, and people “go off into extremist ideologies”, national socialist on one side, communist on the other.
The second runs through resources. If trade fails and you cannot buy the rare earths you need, Shah said, you start to think: “I will bloody march into Africa and I will conquer Africa.” {#march}

~ After 1930 came a Japanese invasion in 1931, Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia in 1935 and Germany’s drive for Lebensraum. *Mein Kampf* predates the tariffs, Shah noted, but they fed a German belief that the trading system was British-controlled and that Germany must conquer land to prosper.

quote.text: There are lines that run from Smoot-Hawley all the way to the second world war.

stories.caption: five biryanis near Mangalore
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a food trip through Mysore and Mangalore
stories.head: Eight meals and a lesson in trade
body: Amit Varma once went on a food trip through Mysore and Mangalore with about 15 friends, many of whom Ajay Shah knows. They took a bus, listed their stops on an Excel sheet and ate something like eight meals a day.
In one area, within a five-kilometre radius of Mangalore, they found five different kinds of biryani. All of them, Varma said, were authentic to the place. {095-S01}
Each had arisen in its own way from the same little area. “This is beautiful,” Varma said. “This is what trade gives you.”
~ The trip closed the first of his cultural arguments for globalisation, that everything Indians eat, wear and say came from elsewhere. That cultural reason, he said, might even be the strongest.
stories.why: What we call authentic local food is the layered result of exchange. Globalisation, in Varma’s telling, shows up in one small area near Mangalore, not just in abstract trade statistics. {095-C08}

stories.caption: the rent-seekers of his youth
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the would-be businessmen of his youth
stories.head: Business plan: befriend the state
body: Jagdish Bhagwati once observed that in China people’s mentality is profit-seeking, while in India it is rent-seeking. {#bhagwati} Amit Varma and a former colleague of Ajay Shah’s once planned to write a piece about it.
Profit-seeking, Varma explained, means making money by bringing value to someone else in a double thank-you moment. Rent-seeking is extractive, such as using a monopoly the state holds.
In all his young years, he said, whenever he met someone who wanted to start a business, he was often shocked by their exploitative mindset. {095-S04}

~ After decades of a closed economy, the path to prosperity ran through the state. Either you became part of it, or you became its crony and got it to put tariffs on your competitors or create entry barriers.

quote.text: If you are open, then you are competing in the global marketplace and you’ll have a profit seeking mentality.

quiz.q: Who coined the phrase “double thank you moment”, and what does it describe?
quiz.a: John Stossel. A voluntary exchange that leaves buyer and seller both better off.

quiz.q: Why should Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma hire a chauffeur, even if they drive best?
quiz.a: Their time and minds are worth more spent on cricket and acting.

quiz.q: In David Ricardo’s example, what did England and Portugal make and trade?
quiz.a: Cloth and wine; by specialising, both countries end up with more of each.

quiz.q: What did Norman Angell argue in *The Great Illusion*, published in 1909?
quiz.a: That war was now impossible, since nations were too intertwined by trade.

quiz.q: A 100-rupee import carries a 10 per cent tariff and sells for 110. Who pays the extra?
quiz.a: The Indian consumer. Exporters don’t pay tariffs; a country’s own buyers do.

quiz.q: Whose trade deficit with his babysitter shows that a deficit need not mean a loss?
quiz.a: Tim Harford’s. He pays her, she buys nothing from him, and both gain.
